newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Analysts doubt BolsWessanen bid talk.
newsitem.headline: Analysts doubt BolsWessanen bid talk.

text.p: Shares in Dutch food and drinks group BolsWessanen NV climbed on Wednesday on reports of a potential takeover, but the company is hardly a juicy target for would-be predators, Dutch analysts said.
BolsWessanen shares were 1.40 guilders higher at 30.00 at 1350 GMT despite a statement from the company saying it had no indication that it would be subject to a takeover bid.
British drinks concern Grand Metropolitan and Dutch trading group Hagemeyer have both been put in the frame for a putative bid.
"The value of BolsWessanen is overestimated," said Suez Kooijman analyst Nico van Geest, pointing to shrinking drinks markets worldwide and concerns about other existing brands.
"The problem is they have weak brands in growth markets and strong brands in weak markets, so its really neither fish nor flesh and certainly not that attractive (for takeover)," he said.

In August BolsWessanen reported first half net income from ordinary activities of 68.9 million guilders ($40.7 million), down 22 percent from the same period in 1995, but said it expected to more than halve the profit fall over the full year.

Amstgeld analyst Marius Andre said he considered the company a "hold" on fundamentals but, with the share price lagging, speculators could be after the stock in the hope of a major development like a bid.
"But I think the company is trying to reshape itself and it would not easily be taken over. The company itself is really not looking for that and it couldn't be done on a friendly basis," he said.
Drinks firm Bols merged with food and dairy concern Wessanen in 1993, intending to use the high margins and earnings of Bols to expand in Wessanen's markets.
But van Geest said the group had largely failed in its ambitions.

"The U.S. business is relatively fine but they are really too small a player in dairy over there and the same applies to cheese in Europe. They have quite a strong position but there's an awful lot of competition and it's quite a mature market."
"They are too late in the emerging markets as well. It's just not exciting."
The low growth potential of BolsWessanen's core activities has been a major problem for the group, analysts said.
It has struggled to find sizeable acquisitions in growing markets to meet its target of 10 percent yearly earnings growth.
But a break-up scenario might be more realistic than a takeover, they said.
"There could be attractive add-ons for other companies there," van Geest said.
